claims.text: Pre-coating tungsten particles with a nanoscale nickel layer will enhance copper wettability at W–Cu interfaces.
A nanoscale nickel interlayer will improve interfacial bonding between tungsten and copper.
Nickel coating will reduce void formation and phase separation in W–Cu composites.
The Ni-modified W–Cu composite will preserve mechanical durability under irradiation.
The proposed initial feedstock consists of tungsten particles or interconnected tungsten regions dispersed within a copper matrix.
Such W–Cu feedstock is typically produced by vapor coating W powders.
A 20–50 nm nickel coating can be applied to tungsten particles by electroless plating, electroplating, or chemical vapor deposition.
The Ni-coated particles can be mixed with copper and consolidated by spark-plasma sintering below approximately 1200 °C.
A controlled reducing atmosphere and controlled heating profile will avoid or limit copper evaporation during consolidation.
The nickel interlayer forms a chemically compatible, low-energy interface at the W–Cu boundary.
The nickel interlayer promotes capillary infiltration and diffusive bonding at the W–Cu boundary.
Improved infiltration and diffusive bonding minimize interfacial voids and defects.
Nickel reduces the surface-energy mismatch between tungsten and copper.
Reduced surface-energy mismatch improves capillary action and diffusion during sintering, producing a more uniform and less porous microstructure.
The nickel layer serves as a diffusion barrier that mitigates intermetallic reactions.
Mitigating intermetallic reactions prevents degradation of thermal transport and mechanical stability under irradiation.
Relative to vapor-coated W-powder composites without nickel modification, the Ni-coated composite will have a lower void fraction and greater microstructural uniformity.
Relative to that baseline, the Ni-coated composite will have higher thermal conductivity.
Relative to that baseline, the Ni-coated composite will retain better mechanical integrity during thermal cycling and irradiation.
The intervention is applicable to fusion-reactor joint heat-transfer components consolidated below approximately 1200 °C and exposed to high heat flux, irradiation, and thermal cycling.

contradictions.description: The initial state is described as an already prefabricated W-in-Cu composite, whereas the intervention requires coating free W particles before they are mixed with copper. The intervention therefore occurs before, rather than on, the stated initial material.

The named baseline uses vapor-coated W powders consolidated by spark-plasma sintering, but the experimental control uses uncoated W particles. Unless the vapor coating is explicitly defined as absent or otherwise reproduced, the control does not match the named baseline.
